To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a single amino substitution in the Nipah virus V protein (V(AAHL)) is responsible for its loss of IFN-antagonist activity and that the V protein is functional as an IFNB antagonist in cells of different species.
a single amino-acid substitution in the V(AAHL) protein prevents it from interacting with STAT1 and 2, and that this is the reason for its failure to antagonize IFNs.

a single amino acid mutation in the V protein is responsible for loss of function of the V protein as an IFN-antagonist in human, monkey and rabbit cells, and that the ability of the V protein to block the IFN response is not a constraint that prevents NiV from crossing species barriers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of the interaction between a paramyxoviral V protein and STAT1 and STAT 2, and its role in IFN antagonism in cells of different species.
a novel mechanism of antagonism of the host IFN response and the role of this function in NiV infection.
understanding how NiV V antagonizes IFN signalling, and how this may affect the pathogenesis of this emerging disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the V protein of NiV is a key determinant in the host range of the virus.
the ability of the V protein to interact with and inhibit STAT1 and STAT 2 is a critical determinant for the IFN-antagonistic function of this protein.
the V(AAHL) mutant of NiV V protein has a single amino acid mutation that is responsible for its inability to interact with STAT proteins and to antagonize IFNs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the V protein of the NiV is able to block the IFN signalling in cells of different species, but a single amino acid change is sufficient to abolish its ability to antagonize the IFN response in human cells.
a single amino acids substitution in the NiV V(AAHL) protein, that is unable to interact with STAT proteins, is responsible for its inability to inhibit the IFN response.
the ability of a virus to block the IFN response is a key factor that determines whether a virus is able to cross a species barrier.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NiV V is an effective IFN antagonist in all species examined to date, which suggests that NiV V may be a useful target for antiviral drug development.
the V protein of a pathogenic paramyxovirus, such as Nipah virus, is able to function as an IFN-antagonist in cells from different mammalian species.
NiV V is able to antagonize IFNs in cells from different animal species.
